content: Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining today — really glad you're all here. My name's Alex, and I'll be guiding the conversation this afternoon. We've got about 45 minutes together, and the main thing I want to say upfront is that this is genuinely a conversation — there's no agenda I'm trying to steer you toward, no right answers I'm looking for. I'm just here to listen and to keep things moving. Whatever you think, whatever your experience is, that's what's useful. If something someone else says connects with your own experience — or doesn't, and you see it differently — just jump in. You don't need to wait to be asked. We will be recording the session for research purposes, so just bear that in mind, but otherwise treat it as a relaxed chat. Okay — let's start nice and simply. If you could just go around and say your name and where in the UK you're coming from today, that'd be great.
Right, yeah — I'm Gregor, I'm from the North West, just outside Manchester actually. Been here most of my life. Good to meet you all.
Yeah, I'm Mark. I'm from out in the countryside, East of England — a village out that way. Been here quite a long time as well, so I know the area pretty well. Nice to meet everyone.

Yeah, hi everyone. I'm James. I'm down in the South East, suburban area — just outside London actually. So a bit different from you two, I'd say. More built up where I am, bit more... I don't know, spread out maybe? Lots of commuters, that sort of thing. But yeah, good to be here.

Great — Manchester, East Anglia, and just outside London. Good spread. Okay, let's get into it. First thing I want to ask is about where you actually spend time with your male friends — like, if you've got a favourite spot in your area, somewhere you tend to end up with the lads, what is it? What makes it that place?

Yeah, for me it's the same really — there's a pub just near the station, and that's where we all end up. It's convenient, innit. Most of us are coming from work or heading home anyway, so it just makes sense. You can grab a pint, have a chat, doesn't have to be anything fancy. And everyone knows the place, so there's no faffing about trying to decide where to go. It's just... where people naturally land.

Yeah, it's a bit different out where I am. There isn't really a station like that, so you don't get that natural gathering point, you know? If I'm meeting up with mates it's more... you've got to actually decide where you're going. Could be the pub in the village, but honestly a lot of the time we just end up at someone's place — someone's got a bit of space, or we'll go to a mate's farm or something. It's less about convenience and more just about, well, where makes sense for everyone that night. Less footfall through naturally I suppose, so there's not that default spot you all just end up at.

Fair point, actually. I hadn't thought of it that way. The station pub thing — yeah, it's dead convenient, but you're right, it does mean you're not really planning it. It's just, oh, Friday after work, everyone's there anyway. Whereas if you've got to actually choose, like you're saying, maybe you end up somewhere that's better for actually talking? Or someone's place where you can properly relax without the noise.

I mean, don't get me wrong, the pub works fine most of the time. But I suppose there's something to be said for having to make a bit more effort. You probably end up having better conversations when it's not just the default spot you drift into.

Exactly, yeah. At someone's place or out at a farm or whatever, you can actually hear each other talk, can't you? The pub's fine, but it's always got that background noise — you're shouting over people, telly's on, all that. When you're sitting at a mate's kitchen table or out in the open air somewhere, you actually have a proper conversation. You know what I mean? There's no distraction, so you end up talking about things that matter a bit more, not just the surface stuff. It feels different. You've made the effort to get there, so maybe you're all a bit more present as well.

Yeah, I get what you're saying. And you're right — the conversations are probably better when you're not dodging the jukebox and someone's shouting about the match. I can see that.

But I'll be honest, at my age with work and family stuff, the convenience thing isn't just... it's not laziness, is it? It's what actually keeps you in touch with people. If I had to plan it all out every time, organize transport, make sure everyone's free on a specific night — I'm not sure I'd do it as much. The station pub, you just fall into it naturally, and that's the thing that actually happens, you know?

So yeah, maybe the conversations aren't as deep. But it's the difference between seeing your mates every other week and... well, not seeing them as much. I think there's something to be said for the regular contact, even if it's a bit more surface level. Keeps the connection going.
Gregor, what about you — where do you tend to end up with your mates?

Yeah, I'm a bit of a mix of both really, to be honest. I've got a couple of regular pubs I'll go to — one or two that we tend to gravitate toward — but I wouldn't say it's quite as default as James describes, and it's not as spread out as what Mark's saying either. Being in the city but not right in the centre, there's just... a few places that work, you know? You might text a mate and say meet at the Ivy or wherever, and everyone knows roughly where that is.

But I think James has got a point there about convenience. You get older, you've got stuff on — work, family bits and pieces — and the easier it is to actually meet up, the more likely you'll do it. I'm not going to pretend I'm having these deep philosophical conversations at the bar every time either. Some nights it's just a pint and a chat about work or football or whatever.

That said, I do sometimes end up at a mate's place, and yeah, you can actually hear yourself think, which is nice. But I wouldn't romanticize it too much — sometimes you want the buzz of being around people, having that background noise, not just sitting round a kitchen table in silence, you know? Different things at different times.

Yeah, that idea of different things at different times makes sense — sometimes you want the buzz, sometimes you want to actually hear yourself think. Right, let's shift gears a bit. I want to ask you something more directly about food. How do you each decide what to eat — day to day, whether that's cooking at home, grabbing something at work, going out? What actually drives what ends up on the plate?

For me it's pretty straightforward really. I eat meat most days — red meat, fish, bit of chicken — and that's just what I've always done. It's filling, it tastes good, and it's what I know how to cook without thinking too much about it. 

I'm not one of those people who sits down and plans the week out or anything. If I'm cooking at home, I'll do a steak or a bit of salmon, maybe a roast on a Sunday. At work I'll grab something with meat in it if I can. It's reliable, innit? You know where you are with it.

I suppose I don't really overthink it. Some people get very worked up about food choices these days, but for me it's just... what do I fancy eating that day? Can I make it easily? Does it fill me up? That's about it. Meat ticks those boxes, so that's what tends to happen.

Yeah, I'd say it's similar for me, but maybe I'd put it slightly differently. I eat meat most days too — chicken, bit of fish, red meat maybe once a week. It's what I grew up with, what my mum cooked, what you just... do, isn't it? So there's a lot of habit in there, not just the practical stuff.

But I think there's more going on than just "does it fill me up." Like, you say you don't overthink it, Gregor, and fair enough — I don't sit down with a spreadsheet either. But we're making choices all the time without really thinking about why. It's convenient because the shops stock it, it's familiar because we've eaten it since we were kids, it's what mates have round for a barbecue. There's culture in there too, not just taste and convenience.

That said, I'm not claiming I've examined all that deeply myself. I just... I notice there's more to it than we sometimes admit, you know? Like, I could eat something else, and I do sometimes. It's not like meat's the only thing that fills you up. But yeah, it's the default for me as well.

Yeah, fair point actually. You're right — there is more going on than just practicality. I mean, I grew up eating meat too, that's just what was on the table, so yeah, there's definitely habit wrapped up in it. And you're spot on about the culture bit — barbecues, Sunday roasts, all that. That's not nothing, is it?

I suppose when I said I don't overthink it, what I meant was I'm not sitting there agonizing over every choice. But you're right that I'm not making these decisions in a vacuum either. It's convenient partly because that's what's everywhere, and it's what I'm used to, and yeah, maybe it's what feels... normal, for lack of a better word. That's all tied together, isn't it?

I do sometimes eat other things — I'll have a vegetarian meal now and then, pasta or whatever — but meat's the go-to. And I think part of that is just... it's familiar. Doesn't feel like I'm having to think about it or make some sort of statement about it. It just is what it is.

But I take your point. There's more cultural stuff baked into it than I was making out. I just don't think that means I need to pick it apart every time I'm deciding what to have for dinner, you know? I'm comfortable with it.

Yeah, no, I get that. You don't want to turn every meal into some kind of moral inventory, that'd drive you mad. But I think there's a difference between that and never stepping back to actually think about it, isn't there?

Like, you've just done it now — you've said, oh yeah, there's habit, there's culture, it's everywhere so that's why it feels normal. You've picked it apart a bit, and it made sense, didn't it? You didn't get agonized about it, you just... understood your own patterns a bit better. That's not the same as overthinking every plate of food you eat.

I think I'm in the same boat, honestly. I'm not going to sit there analyzing my lunch. But every now and then you notice something — like, oh right, I always do this because I've always done this, not because I've actually decided. And that's okay to notice, isn't it? Doesn't mean you have to change anything. Just means you're not doing it completely on autopilot.

For me it's fine. Meat works, I eat it, I'm comfortable with it. But I'm also aware that's partly just... what I'm used to. And yeah, that's how most of us are, I'd say.
Mark, you've been quiet on this one — what does it look like for you? How do you end up deciding what to eat?

Yeah, I'm much the same really. Meat most days — I'll have red meat maybe once a week, fish once a week, chicken as well. And yeah, it's just... that's what you do, innit? It's familiar. I grew up with it, my family ate it, and it's what I cook at home.

I suppose I don't really sit and think about it much either. You go to the butcher or the supermarket, you know what you're after, you cook it. It fills you up, tastes good, you know how to do it without having to consult a recipe or anything. 

James's point about culture and habit — yeah, I'd say that's right. It's baked in. But like Gregor says, I'm not going to agonize over it. I eat what I eat, and I'm comfortable with that. It works for me.

Thanks Mark. So across the three of you there's a pretty consistent thread — meat's the default, it's familiar, it's what you grew up with, and that's mostly just... comfortable. That's useful context. I want to move on to something related but slightly different. Do you think your gender influences what you eat? Why, or why not?

I think it probably does, yeah. Or at least... it's hard to separate out, isn't it? Growing up out in the countryside, farming's a big part of the culture, and that's definitely a male thing in a lot of families. You know, working with animals, raising livestock — that's what your dad did, your grandfather did. So meat's not just food, it's tied to that whole world.

And I suppose there's an expectation, or just the way things are — blokes eat meat, that's sort of the baseline. You go to a barbecue, the men are cooking the steaks. You have a roast on Sunday, that's the centerpiece. I'm not saying anyone's ever given me grief about it or anything, but it's just... that's the pattern, isn't it? That's what's normal in the farming communities round here.

Whether that's me being influenced by that or just how things naturally are, I couldn't really say. Probably a bit of both. But yeah, I'd say gender's in there somewhere. It's wrapped up with being a bloke from round here, I think.

Yeah, I think there's something in that, though it plays out a bit differently where I am. Mark's talking about farming and all that — that's a real tangible thing, isn't it? But even in the city, there's still this idea that... I dunno, that blokes just eat meat, don't they? It's not a big deal, it's not something you have to justify or think about too much.

And I think there's a bit of — if you start getting fussy about what you eat, asking questions about it, maybe considering alternatives or whatever, there's this underlying thing where that doesn't quite feel... masculine, maybe? Like, you're overthinking it, or being a bit precious about your food. Real blokes just eat what's put in front of them, don't make a fuss.

I'm not saying that's how I think it should be or anything, but I notice it. You see someone order a salad or say they don't eat much meat, and there's always that little... something. A joke, or a raised eyebrow, or someone asks why. With a woman ordering the same thing, nobody bats an eyelid.

So yeah, I reckon gender's in there. Not in the same way as the farming thing Mark's talking about, but it's there. It's about not wanting to be seen as overthinking things, being awkward about it. Just eating what you eat and not making a production out of it — that feels like the normal thing to do, doesn't it?

Yeah, that rings true, actually. The not wanting to stand out bit — I think that's real. Out where I am, if you started saying you weren't eating meat or you were going vegetarian or whatever, people would notice. They'd ask questions, make comments. And yeah, there's that edge to it, isn't there? Like you're making some kind of statement about yourself, or being difficult.

But I'm not entirely sure how much of that is actually... I don't know, natural masculinity or whatever, and how much is just us all accepting the way things are without really questioning it. Like Gregor says, you don't want to be fussy, you don't want to seem like you're overthinking things. But that's quite a tight box to stay in, when you think about it. You're just eating what you eat because that's what blokes do, and if you deviate from that, you're making it a thing.

I'm not saying I've got it all worked out or anything. I eat meat because I like it and it's what I'm used to. But the social side of it — yeah, there's definitely pressure there to just go along with it without questioning too much. Whether that's because it's actually more masculine or just because we've all decided that's how it is... I'm honestly not sure.

Right, yeah — that's the thing that gets me a bit, actually. Because I do like meat, I'm not going to pretend otherwise. It's satisfying, I enjoy cooking it, I'd miss it if it was gone. That's genuine.

But there's this... I dunno, it feels like you're not allowed to just sit with that without it becoming a whole thing. Like, I can say I like eating meat, but the minute you start asking why, or thinking about where it comes from, or even just noticing that yeah, there's this cultural expectation wrapped around it — suddenly you're being difficult or woke or whatever people say.

It's almost like the only way to be a bloke about it is to just not examine it at all. Just eat it, don't ask questions, don't engage with the fact that there's more going on than "it tastes good." And I'm not saying I sit around pondering my dinner every night, but I do notice it, you know? I notice that I can't really have a conversation about why I eat meat without someone getting defensive or making it into some kind of statement about my identity.

Mark's right — it is a tight box. And I'm not sure that's actually about being naturally masculine or whatever. I think it's more about... well, nobody wants to rock the boat. So we all just go along with it and don't ask too many questions, and that becomes the normal. But then you can't actually think about your own choices without it feeling risky somehow.

That feels a bit off to me, to be honest.
James, you've been listening to all of this — does any of it land with you, coming from where you are?

Yeah, it does, actually. What Gregor's saying at the end there — that feels right to me. The tight box thing, the sense that you can't just... examine your own choices without it becoming something bigger than it is.

I mean, where I'm from, it's not the farming thing like Mark's got going on. It's more diffuse, isn't it? But there's still this underlying thing that you eat meat, you don't make a fuss about it, you certainly don't start getting all questioning about it. That's just not what blokes do.

And what gets me is — I don't think that's actually about being masculine. I think it's just laziness, honestly. It's easier to not think about it. And the minute someone does start asking questions — even just for themselves, not to make a point — suddenly there's all this defensiveness. People act like you're attacking them or something.

But the thing is, you can like meat and still notice what's going on culturally, can't you? Those aren't mutually exclusive. I eat meat because I genuinely don't have a strong pull against it. But I also think it's a bit embarrassing when people act like even acknowledging that there's culture and expectation wrapped up in it is somehow... I don't know, a threat to them or something. It just is what it is. We make choices based on habit and what's around us and what feels normal. That's human, not weak.

That's a useful place to have got to — this idea that you can genuinely like something and still notice there's a whole layer of social pressure telling you not to think too carefully about it. Let me build on that actually, because it connects to something I want to ask you about. Imagine for a moment that you did decide to go plant-based — not because anyone's telling you to, just imagine you made that choice. What would actually need to change in your life for that to be possible?

Well, that's the practical bit, isn't it? I mean, first off — I'd need to actually know how to cook without meat. That's not nothing. I can do a steak, a bit of fish, roast chicken, all that. But beans and lentils and whatever else? I'd have to learn. I'd have to actually think about what I'm cooking every night instead of just... doing what I know.

And then there's the shopping side of it. I know where to go for decent meat — butcher in the village, supermarket's fine. But I'd have to figure out where you get good veg, whether it's even available out where I am, whether it's actually affordable. Round here it's not like you've got a farmers' market on every corner.

But honestly, the biggest thing would be the... I don't know how to put it. The social side. If I stopped eating meat, people would ask why. You'd get comments at a barbecue, or when you're having dinner at someone's place. Your mates would notice. And you'd feel like you had to have an answer ready, you know? Like you were making some kind of choice about it, some kind of statement. And I'm not sure I'd want to deal with that.

I like meat, so I'm not going to do it. But if I did — yeah, it would take some effort. Not just practically, but... socially as well. You'd have to be prepared for it to be a thing.

Yeah, but here's the thing — and I'm not having a go at you, Mark — but you're listing all these barriers without actually asking yourself what you'd gain from it, or what you'd miss. Like, you'd have to learn to cook differently, fair enough. But you'd also be learning to cook, wouldn't you? That's not... that's not nothing in a bad way.

And the social cost thing — look, I get it, people would comment. They probably would. But I wonder if you're overestimating that a bit, because you're imagining it as this big declaration you're making. Whereas actually, you could just... eat differently without turning it into a statement, couldn't you? You could say you're trying something, or you just fancy it, or you're not even sure yet. It doesn't have to be this whole thing.

What gets me is — you're already saying you'd miss meat. You like it. So that's a real trade-off, and that's honest. But all the other stuff, the cooking, the shopping, the social bit — those feel like they're about fear of change more than actual barriers, if I'm being blunt. And I notice you're not even sitting with what might appeal to you about it. Like, what if you discovered you actually enjoyed cooking something new? What if you found out the veg round here is fine, or better than you thought?

I'm not saying you should go plant-based or anything. But the way you're framing it — it's all obstacle, no curiosity. And I think that's partly the tight box thing we were just talking about, you know? You're not even letting yourself be curious about it without it feeling like a threat.

Fair point, some of that. You're right — I'm not being particularly curious about it, am I? And yeah, learning to cook differently, that's not a bad thing necessarily. I do enjoy cooking, actually. So that bit's fair.

But I think you're underestimating the social side a bit, Gregor. It's not just... oh, people might comment. It's more than that out where I am. It's tied to who you are, what you do, how people know you. If I started eating differently, it wouldn't just be a quiet personal choice. People would want to know why. And in a village, that gets around. It becomes part of how people think about you.

That's not fear of change exactly. It's just... real. It's the actual social fabric of where I live. You can say oh, just tell them you're trying something, but that works differently in a place like London or Manchester, doesn't it? Round here, there's a smaller circle, and things mean something different.

But look — you're right that I'm not being curious. I'm not sitting with it, I'm not wondering what I might enjoy about it. And that's partly what you're saying, isn't it? That I'm not even letting myself think about it properly because it feels risky. And yeah, that's true. But that doesn't mean the risk isn't real. It's just... I know my context. I know what would happen.

I like meat though. That's genuine. So it's not like I'm white-knuckling my way through meals wishing I could eat something else. I'm actually comfortable with how I eat. The curiosity thing — fair enough. But the change itself? I'm not sure it's worth it to me.
James, you've been listening to this — what's your take?

I think you're both right, actually, and I think you're both missing something as well.

Mark, I get what you're saying about the village thing — the social fabric, people knowing you, it mattering. That's real. But I also think Gregor's got a point that you're maybe... catastrophizing it a bit? Like, you're imagining this massive reaction, but you haven't actually tested it. You might be surprised.

That said, Gregor, I think you're being a bit harsh about the fear thing. It's not just that Mark's being incurious or stuck in a box. There's a real difference between where you live and where he lives. Out in the countryside, that stuff genuinely does matter more. It's not the same as the city where you can kind of fade into the background. Mark knows his community. That's not nothing.

But here's what I'd say — and maybe this is just me being suburban and trying to sit in the middle — I don't think any of this is actually about whether plant-based eating is a threat or whatever. I think it's just that we're all, all three of us, quite invested in not having to think too hard about our choices. And so when someone asks us to imagine changing, we immediately reach for all the reasons why we can't. Not because they're all stupid reasons, but because the easier thing is to just... not change. Not even be curious about it.

I eat meat, I'm fine with it. But I could probably eat less of it, or differently, if I fancied it. The fact that I don't think about it much — that's partly genuine comfort, and it's partly just... habit. And maybe that's okay. But we shouldn't pretend it's more inevitable than it is.

James, that last bit — 'we shouldn't pretend it's more inevitable than it is' — that's a useful place to leave it. So if it's not inevitable, let's think about what might actually make it feel more appealing or realistic. Not what would force you into it — more like: what would genuinely make plant-based food feel like a better option? Either for yourselves or for other men you know.

Yeah, that question's landing a bit differently now, actually. Because James is right — I was sitting here pointing out Mark's blind spots without looking at my own. And he's also right that I'm maybe underestimating how much easier it is to just not think about it.

So if we're talking about what would actually make it feel more appealing to me... I dunno, honest answer? Probably if it didn't feel like such a shift, you know? Like, if the stuff was just... there. Normal. If I could go to the shop and grab something plant-based that was as straightforward as picking up a steak, that tasted as good, filled you up the same way — no faffing about with recipes or feeling like you're making some kind of statement by eating it.

And maybe if it wasn't so tied up with all the cultural baggage. Because right now, when someone says plant-based, it comes with this whole... thing attached to it. Like you're either making a moral point or you're being difficult or you're trying to be trendy or whatever. If it was just... food, you know? An option that didn't make you feel like you had to justify yourself or defend your masculinity or whatever — that would make it easier to actually think about.

I'm not saying I'd switch over. I actually do like meat, that's not bullshit. But I think I could be more curious about it if it didn't feel so loaded. Does that make sense? Like, the barriers aren't really about the food itself for me. It's more about what choosing it would mean, in a way.

You know what, though — listening to myself just now, I'm doing the same thing Mark was doing, aren't I? I'm saying oh, if the culture was different, if it was normalized, then maybe I'd think about it. But that's just another way of saying I don't want to be the one to step outside the line, isn't it? 

I'm blaming all the external stuff — the baggage, the expectations — but really I'm just... comfortable. And I'm using those barriers as a reason not to actually sit with what I'd actually miss if I changed, or what I might gain. Because the truth is, I could probably try eating differently right now if I wanted to. I don't need everyone else to normalize it first.

The thing that's a bit uncomfortable is — I actually quite like meat. Like, genuinely. It's not just habit for me, it's something I'd miss. So if I'm being honest with myself, the reason I'm not curious about changing isn't really about the culture or what people would think. It's that I don't actually want to give it up enough to deal with the inconvenience of learning something new.

And that's fine, right? That's a legitimate choice. But I shouldn't dress it up as oh, if only the world was different. The world isn't going to change to make it easier for me. I'm just... okay with things as they are. And maybe I should just own that instead of pretending there's all this external stuff in the way.

Gregor, I appreciate that — that's a pretty honest place to land. James, Mark — does that resonate with you, or does it land differently? What would actually make plant-based food more appealing to you, if anything?

Yeah, I... listening to you say that, Gregor, it does land differently for me, actually. Because I think what you're saying is true for you, but I'm not sure it's the same for me, and I need to sit with that a bit.

You're right that I've been hiding behind the social thing. And some of that is real — the village context is real. But you're also right that I could probably try things without it being this massive declaration. And I haven't really... I haven't actually asked myself properly, do I want to change? Or am I just defending the choice I've already made?

And honest answer? I don't know. I like meat, that's genuine. I cook it, I enjoy it. I'd miss it. But I also... I don't actually know if I'm comfortable with how much I've just not thought about it. Like, I've made it all about the social barriers, but some of that's because thinking about it differently feels uncomfortable, and it's easier to blame the village or whatever.

If you asked me what would make plant-based appealing — I'm not sure I've even got a good answer, because I haven't really let myself wonder about it, have I? I've just... shut it down. Said no, not for me, too much hassle, people would notice. But that's partly me not being curious, like you said.

I don't think I'm going to go plant-based. But maybe I should at least ask myself why, properly, instead of just... listing reasons it won't work.

Yeah, and I think there's something different going on with you though, Mark. Because you're saying you haven't really let yourself be curious — and that's fair, you're being honest about it — but I wonder if it's not quite the same as what I just worked through.

Like, for me, I've actually thought about it. I know I like meat, I know what I'd miss. I'm just comfortable enough that I'm not going to change. That's a choice I've made, even if I wasn't fully conscious of it.

But you — I think you've actually shut down the thinking part earlier. It's not just that you've made a choice and you're okay with it. You've kind of... not let yourself get to the point where you could make that choice properly, you know? You've blocked it at the thinking stage because the social thing feels so real and so loaded that you haven't even got to the part where you ask yourself what you actually want.

And I'm wondering if that's partly because the social stakes genuinely are higher where you are. Like, it's not just about you being curious or not curious. It's that being curious in that context feels risky in a way it maybe isn't for me. So you've preemptively shut it down to protect yourself from that risk.

Which is... I don't know, it feels different from just being comfortable with your choice. It feels more like you're defending against something. And I'm not sure that's actually serving you, if that makes sense. Not saying you should change anything. But just... maybe worth sitting with that difference?
James, you've been quiet while these two have been working through something — what's your read on it?

I think Gregor's right, actually — there is something different going on with Mark. And I think he's being fair about it, not harsh.

But I also want to say something about what Gregor just did, because I noticed it. You worked through something honest there, mate — you owned that you're just comfortable, you don't need the world to change for you. That's fair. But then you kind of... turned that into advice for Mark, didn't you? Like you'd figured it out and now you're helping him see his blind spot.

And maybe that's true. But I'm wondering if you're also... I don't know, using what you just learned about yourself to feel a bit better about it? Like, oh, I've thought about it properly, I know what I want, I'm being honest. So now I can help Mark see that he hasn't thought about it at all.

Which might be true. But it also means you're not sitting with the uncomfortable bit anymore, you know? You've moved past it. You've made your peace with it.

For Mark, I think you're right — he has shut it down early. The social thing where he is, that's real. But I also think there's something else going on, which is that he doesn't actually want to be curious about it right now. And that might be fine. That might be a legitimate choice too. But he doesn't need to convince himself that it's because the barriers are too high. He could just... not be interested. And that would be okay.
